title: JPA and Hibernate entities
intro: With JPA, you can work with Java objects while connecting them to tables in the database. In this lesson, we will look at how entities, relationships and repositories work, and why you need to be careful with the queries generated by the ORM.
body:
## What is ORM?

ORM, or **Object-Relational Mapping**, is a technique that connects object-oriented programming with relational databases.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Objects in, SQL out", "nodes": [{"id": "svc", "label": "TaskService", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "repo", "label": "TaskRepository", "sub": "extends JpaRepository"}, {"id": "hib", "label": "Hibernate", "sub": "persistence context", "highlight": true}, {"id": "db", "label": "PostgreSQL", "kind": "db"}], "edges": [{"from": "svc", "to": "repo", "label": "save(task)"}, {"from": "repo", "to": "hib"}, {"from": "hib", "to": "db", "label": "INSERT / UPDATE"}, {"from": "db", "to": "hib", "label": "rows → @Entity", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

On the Java side, for example, you might have a `User` class and a `Task` class. In the database, these could correspond to a `users` and a `tasks` table.

Without an ORM, you would have to write SQL queries yourself and manually convert the results into Java objects. With an ORM, the framework handles part of this relationship for you.

In the Spring Boot world, **Hibernate** is very commonly used for this purpose. Hibernate is an ORM framework, while **JPA (Jakarta Persistence API)** is a specification that defines how persistent Java objects are managed.

Think about it simply like this:

~~~text
Java object  <->  JPA/Hibernate  <->  SQL  <->  PostgreSQL
~~~

For example, a Java object like this:

~~~java
User user = new User();
user.setName("Anna");
~~~

can correspond to a database record like this:

~~~sql
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Anna');
~~~

In certain situations, Hibernate can generate this SQL automatically.

### Advantages of ORM

One of the biggest advantages of ORM is that you can primarily work with objects in your application's business logic. You do not need to write SQL for every simple CRUD operation.

Other advantages include:

- You can work with Java types instead of database values directly.
- Relationships can also be represented as objects.
- Spring Data JPA eliminates a lot of repository code.
- Transactions and entity management integrate well with Spring.
- You need less repetitive CRUD code.

### Disadvantages of ORM

ORM is not magic, though. SQL still runs underneath.

This is very important: **just because you do not write SQL does not mean SQL disappears.**

ORM queries can be slow, load too much data, or even generate hundreds of separate SQL queries.

That is why a good backend developer needs to understand SQL even when using JPA.

---

## Adding Spring Data JPA

In a Spring Boot application, JPA support is provided by the `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` dependency.

For Maven, for example:

~~~xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
~~~

For PostgreSQL, you also need the PostgreSQL JDBC driver:

~~~xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
~~~

The JDBC driver allows the Java application to communicate with PostgreSQL through JDBC.

The `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`, on the other hand, provides the infrastructure needed to use JPA and Spring Data JPA, and uses Hibernate as the JPA provider by default.

---

## Your first JPA entity

A JPA entity is a Java class that the persistence layer can treat as a database record.

Let's look at the task manager's `User` entity:

~~~java
@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;
}
~~~

`@Entity` tells Hibernate that this class is a persistent entity.

With `@Table`, you can specify which database table the entity belongs to. Here, the Java class is `User`, while the database table is `users`.

`@Id` marks the primary key.

`@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` says that the database generates the ID value. With PostgreSQL, this fits well with the identity columns we mentioned in the previous lesson.

With `@Column`, you can specify additional column settings.

For example:

~~~java
@Column(name = "display_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
private String name;
~~~

Here, the Java field is called `name`, while the database column is called `display_name`.

It is important to understand that annotations do not replace database design. We will still manage the production database schema with controlled migrations.

---

## Relationships between entities

In real applications, entities are rarely completely independent of each other.

For example, in the task manager, a user can have multiple tasks.

~~~text
User
  |
  | 1
  |
  | *
Task
~~~

This is a **one-to-many** relationship.

A task, however, belongs to exactly one user, so we use a `@ManyToOne` relationship on the `Task` side.

~~~java
@Entity
@Table(name = "tasks")
public class Task {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String title;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private boolean done;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id", nullable = false)
    private User user;
}
~~~

`@ManyToOne` means that many tasks can belong to the same user.

`Task` is the **owning side** of the relationship, meaning this side holds the foreign key that represents the relationship. In the database, the `tasks.user_id` column points to `users.id`.

`LAZY` means that Hibernate does not automatically load the related `User` object every time a task is fetched. It only tries to load it when you actually need it, with an appropriate persistence context.

This is generally a better default choice than automatic eager loading, but it does not solve query problems by itself.

The other side of the relationship can look like this:

~~~java
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "user")
private List<Task> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
~~~

`mappedBy = "user"` says that `User.tasks` does not own the relationship. The relationship is managed by the `Task.user` field.

This means the roles of the two sides are different:

| Java side | Annotation | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `Task.user` | `@ManyToOne` | owning side, foreign key is here |
| `User.tasks` | `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "user")` | inverse side |

### Why is mappedBy important?

If you do not understand which side owns the relationship, you can easily create a mapping that results in an unnecessary join table or unwanted database operations.

With a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is typically on the "many" side. That is why `Task` is the owning side.

---

## Spring Data repositories

One of the most convenient parts of Spring Data JPA is the repository abstraction.

For example:

~~~java
public interface TaskRepository extends JpaRepository<Task, Long> {
}
~~~

`JpaRepository<Task, Long>` already provides many basic operations, such as saving, searching, deleting and retrieving by ID.

You do not have to write the entire repository implementation yourself.

### Derived queries

Spring Data JPA can create queries from method names.

~~~java
List<Task> findByUserIdAndDone(Long userId, boolean done);
~~~

Spring Data interprets the conditions based on the method name.

You can think of the logic as roughly equivalent to this SQL:

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = ?
  AND done = ?;
~~~

This is very practical for simple queries.

For more complex cases, you can use an explicit JPQL query with the `@Query` annotation:

~~~java
@Query("SELECT t FROM Task t WHERE t.user.id = :userId AND t.done = false")
List<Task> findOpenTasks(@Param("userId") Long userId);
~~~

JPQL does not work directly with database table names. Instead, it works with entities and their fields.

Hibernate turns this into the appropriate SQL.

---

## Why shouldn't you return an entity from a controller?

Technically, you could do this:

~~~java
@GetMapping
public List<Task> getTasks() {
    return taskRepository.findAll();
}
~~~

But in a production application, this is generally not the best approach.

The controller should instead return a DTO.

~~~java
public record TaskResponse(
    Long id,
    String title,
    boolean done,
    String userName
) {}
~~~

There are several reasons for this.

First, the entity is part of the database persistence model, while the DTO is part of the API contract. It is better not to mix the two.

Second, when returning entities, you can easily run into problems with lazy relationships or accidentally load too much data.

Third, with a bidirectional relationship, JSON serialization can even create a circular structure:

~~~text
User -> tasks -> user -> tasks -> user -> ...
~~~

A DTO precisely defines what you want to send to the API client.

---

## The N+1 query problem

One of the most important JPA problems is the **N+1 query** problem.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "N+1 queries", "lang": "sql", "code": "SELECT * FROM orders;          -- 1\nSELECT * FROM customer WHERE id=1;\nSELECT * FROM customer WHERE id=2;\n-- … one per order (N)", "note": "A lazy relation loaded inside a loop: 101 queries for 100 orders."}, "right": {"title": "JOIN FETCH", "lang": "java", "code": "@Query(\"\"\"\n  select o from Order o\n  join fetch o.customer\n  \"\"\")\nList<Order> findAllWithCustomer();", "note": "One query brings both — check the SQL log to prove it."}}
~~~

Suppose you fetch 100 tasks:

~~~java
List<Task> tasks = taskRepository.findAll();
~~~

Hibernate may first run a query like this:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title, done, user_id
FROM tasks;
~~~

This is the first query, hence the "1".

Then, in your code, you access the user for every task:

~~~java
for (Task task : tasks) {
    System.out.println(task.getUser().getName());
}
~~~

If the relationship is lazy, Hibernate may issue additional queries to load the users.

You might see SQL like this:

~~~sql
SELECT id, name, email
FROM users
WHERE id = ?;

SELECT id, name, email
FROM users
WHERE id = ?;

SELECT id, name, email
FROM users
WHERE id = ?;
~~~

If 100 tasks result in 100 separate user queries, a total of **101 queries** may run.

This is the N+1 problem.

The code looks simple, but communication with the database can be expensive. It creates network round trips, database load and latency.

---

## Using JOIN FETCH

If you know that you also need the user data for the tasks, you can ask Hibernate to load them in a single query.

For example, with JPQL:

~~~java
@Query("""
    SELECT t
    FROM Task t
    JOIN FETCH t.user
    WHERE t.done = false
""")
List<Task> findOpenTasksWithUser();
~~~

Hibernate may generate SQL similar to this:

~~~sql
SELECT t.id, t.title, t.done, t.user_id,
       u.id, u.name, u.email
FROM tasks t
JOIN users u ON u.id = t.user_id
WHERE t.done = false;
~~~

The important point is that the tasks and the users you need arrive in a single database query.

This can eliminate the N+1 problem in this particular situation.

### EntityGraph

Another option is `@EntityGraph`.

~~~java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "user")
List<Task> findByDoneFalse();
~~~

With `EntityGraph`, you can declaratively specify which related entities you want to load as part of a particular query.

Both approaches are useful. The point is not to use `JOIN FETCH` everywhere, but to understand what SQL you want to achieve.

---

## SQL still matters

Even when using JPA, you should pay attention to the SQL being generated.

During development, you can enable:

~~~properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
~~~

This lets you see the SQL queries generated by Hibernate in the console.

This is especially useful when investigating performance problems.

If you see many similar `SELECT` statements after a single API request, you should investigate whether you are dealing with an N+1 problem.

---

## Why shouldn't you use ddl-auto=update in production?

During development, you may encounter this:

~~~properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
~~~

This tells Hibernate to try to automatically modify the database schema based on the entities.

It can be convenient during local development, but in production you do not want an ORM to try to figure out and modify the database structure when the application starts.

In production, you need controlled, versioned database migrations.

That is why **Flyway** will be the topic of the next lesson. We will look at how to manage database schema changes reproducibly and safely using SQL migrations.

---

## Common mistakes

### Eager relationships everywhere

Do not automatically set every relationship to `EAGER` just because it seems simpler. This can easily cause you to load too much data.

### Returning entities directly

A JPA entity is not the same thing as an API response model. Use DTOs so that you can control your API contract.

### Completely ignoring SQL

If you use JPA, you still need to understand what SQL is being executed. `show-sql` is a simple way to check this during development.

### Using JOIN FETCH for every query

`JOIN FETCH` is a useful tool, but it is not a universal solution. You also need to consider the query result, the number of relationships and the amount of data.

### `ddl-auto=update` in production

Do not rely on automatic Hibernate schema updates to modify a production database. Schema changes should be versioned with migrations.

---

## Summary

JPA and Hibernate significantly reduce the repetitive code required for database access, but they do not hide the performance consequences of the database from you.

The most important idea is this: **the entity model and the database model are connected, but neither is the same as the API model.**

Understand the roles of `@Entity`, `@Id`, `@GeneratedValue`, `@ManyToOne`, `@OneToMany` and `mappedBy`, use repositories for simple queries, and always pay attention to the SQL generated by Hibernate.

In the next lesson, we will approach the other side of the problem: how to manage database schema changes with **Flyway migrations**, so that the same schema can be created reliably in development, testing and production.
takeaways: JPA/Hibernate ORM connects Java objects with a relational database, but SQL still runs underneath the ORM.
The @ManyToOne side is typically the owning side, while @OneToMany(mappedBy = "user") is the inverse side.
With Spring Data JPA repositories, you can create both derived queries and @Query-based queries.
The N+1 problem can cause many unnecessary SQL queries and can be addressed with approaches such as JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
In production, do not rely on ddl-auto=update for schema changes; in the next lesson, we will manage them with Flyway migrations.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of an ORM?
options: Managing the mapping between Java objects and data in a relational database
Automatically installing the PostgreSQL server
Converting frontend components into Java classes
Completely eliminating all SQL queries
quiz.explanation: An ORM such as Hibernate maps Java objects to data stored in a relational database and can generate SQL queries.

quiz.question: In a User–Task relationship, which side is typically the owning side when the tasks table contains the user_id foreign key?
options: User, because one User can have multiple Tasks
Task, because Task contains the foreign key representing the relationship
Both, because JPA always uses two owning sides
Neither, because the repository manages the foreign key
quiz.explanation: The @ManyToOne relationship on the Task side owns the relationship because the tasks.user_id foreign key is located on that side.

quiz.question: What does the N+1 query problem mean in the following situation?
options: A SQL query always returns exactly N+1 rows
Hibernate creates N+1 databases for the same application
An initial query is followed by many additional per-item queries
PostgreSQL automatically runs an INSERT after every SELECT
quiz.explanation: With N+1, one initial query loads the base data, and then additional queries may be executed for individual elements of the result.

quiz.question: Which approach can you use to ask Hibernate to load the Task and its related User in a single query?
options: @Column(nullable = false)
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
Using @EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH
ddl-auto=update
quiz.explanation: Both @EntityGraph and JOIN FETCH can be used to load the required related entities as part of the same query.

quiz.question: Why is it a good idea to return a DTO instead of a JPA entity from a REST controller?
options: Because a DTO automatically generates faster SQL
Because it separates the API response model from the persistence model
Because a JPA entity can never be used as a Java object
Because a DTO means you no longer need a repository
quiz.explanation: A DTO lets you return exactly the data structure the API needs, independently of the database persistence model.

exercise.title: A single JOIN instead of N+1
exercise.task: Write one SQL query that returns every open task together with the user's name. The result must contain exactly the columns `task_id`, `title`, and `user_name`. Only tasks where `done = 0` should be returned. Join `tasks.user_id` to `users.id`, and order the result by `user_name` ascending and then `title` ascending. The query must return all required data in a single result set.
exercise.setup:
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);

INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES
  (1, 'Anna', 'anna@example.com'),
  (2, 'Béla', 'bela@example.com'),
  (3, 'Csilla', 'csilla@example.com'),
  (4, 'Dávid', 'david@example.com');

INSERT INTO tasks (id, title, done, user_id) VALUES
  (1, 'API megtervezése', 0, 1),
  (2, 'README frissítése', 1, 1),
  (3, 'Adatbázis migráció', 0, 2),
  (4, 'Teszt írása', 0, 2),
  (5, 'Frontend javítása', 1, 3),
  (6, 'Hibajegy ellenőrzése', 0, 3),
  (7, 'Deploy előkészítése', 0, 4),
  (8, 'Logolás hozzáadása', 1, 4),
  (9, 'Dokumentáció írása', 0, 1),
  (10, 'Régi task lezárása', 1, 2);
exercise.starter:
SELECT
  t.id AS task_id,
  t.title,
  u.name AS user_name
FROM tasks t
WHERE t.done = 0;
exercise.solution:
SELECT
  t.id AS task_id,
  t.title,
  u.name AS user_name
FROM tasks t
JOIN users u ON u.id = t.user_id
WHERE t.done = 0
ORDER BY u.name ASC, t.title ASC;
exercise.hint: Return the task and user data in one result set. Join `tasks.user_id` to `users.id`, filter for `done = 0`, and order by `user_name` and then `title`.

tests.name: It returns exactly the six open tasks with the correct user names
It returns the data in the required order
It uses one result set for the complete query
